opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of progress to be made here, but I'd be careful not to overestimate how close we are. When I look at the teams I work with that build agentic workflows, much of the work isn't writing the code. It's figuring out how to break a complex task into the right steps, deciding where to use reflection, tool use, planning, or multi-agent collaboration, and then running evals to see where things break.

Parts of that are definitely automatable. Some of the most valuable work right now is error analysis: looking at the traces, finding which step in the pipeline is underperforming, and deciding whether to fix the prompt, swap the model, or restructure the workflow. LLMs are getting quite good at helping with pieces of that. You can have a model read through hundreds of outputs and cluster the failure modes, or propose prompt revisions and test them against an eval set. That kind of automated optimization loop is real, and it's improving quickly.

But the harder part, which I don't think we'll fully automate soon, is the product and domain judgment. Knowing what the workflow should actually do for a customer, what a good output looks like, and what trade-offs among cost, latency, and quality make sense for a specific business still takes a skilled person who understands the problem. One pattern I've seen is that the bottleneck is shifting. Building has become so much faster with AI coding assistants that the scarce resource is increasingly deciding what to build and specifying it clearly.

So my view is that we'll increasingly automate the mechanics of building and tuning agentic workflows, and that will make developers much more productive. The people who do best will be the ones who combine strong AI-building skills with deep domain understanding. Rather than shrinking demand for that kind of engineer, I think it will make each one dramatically more valuable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I'm actually really optimistic about this, but I think it's worth being precise about what's getting automated and what isn't.

When I look at how teams build agentic workflows today, there's a lot of the work that is, frankly, pretty mechanical. Writing the glue code to call a model, parse its output, hand it to the next step, add a retry, wire up a tool. That part, coding assistants are already doing a lot of. I write code with AI assistance every day now, and for that kind of scaffolding it's just much faster. So the cost of producing a first version of an agentic system has fallen dramatically, and I think that trend continues.

But here's the thing I keep seeing with the teams I work with. The hard part of building an agent was never really typing the code. The hard part is figuring out why it isn't working. You build a workflow with, say, five or six steps, you run it, it gets the wrong answer, and the question is, which step broke? Was it the retrieval step pulling the wrong documents? Was it the reasoning step misinterpreting the documents? Was the prompt ambiguous? That debugging loop, looking at traces, building evals, deciding where to put your attention, that's where most of the engineering time actually goes. And that part is much less automated today.

So I think of it as, the implementation layer is getting automated quickly, and the evaluation and error analysis layer is lagging. And honestly, I think the eval piece is the key. When I talk to teams that are struggling, it's rarely because they can't write the code. It's because they don't have a disciplined way to measure whether a change made things better or worse, so they're flying blind. If you have good evals, then you can have an AI system propose a change, run the evals, and tell you whether it helped. That closes the loop. Without the evals, you can't really hand the work off, to a person or to a machine.

Longer term, I do think we'll get agents that help build agents, where you describe a workflow and the system drafts the architecture, instruments it, and proposes evals. We're already seeing early versions of that. But I'd push back a little on the framing that the engineering goes away. What happens is the engineering moves up a level. You spend less time on the plumbing and more time deciding what the system should do, what good looks like, and where it's failing. And that's a skill that I think more people should learn, not fewer, because the leverage you get from being able to direct these systems is just enormous right now.

astra-6.text:
I’m optimistic about it. A lot of the work in building an agent workflow is itself work that AI can help with: writing integrations, testing prompts, looking at failures, and revising the system. So there’s an opportunity to use agents to help build agents.

But I think the harder part is figuring out what to improve. If a workflow gives you a bad answer, did the model misunderstand the task? Did retrieval bring back the wrong information? Did a tool fail? An engineer has to break that down and develop an evaluation that tells you whether a change actually helped. We can automate more of that process, but you still need a clear definition of success.

So I expect increasing amounts of the implementation and experimentation to become automated. That makes engineering judgment—choosing the right problem, setting up useful evaluations, and knowing which failures matter—even more valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic. Building an agent workflow today involves a lot of engineering: connecting tools, managing context, deciding when to retry, and figuring out where things went wrong. AI can help write that code, but I think it can also help with the iteration process itself.

For example, you might start with a workflow, run it on a set of tasks, and inspect the failures. Was the information retrieval poor? Did the agent choose the wrong tool? Did it misunderstand the tool’s output? If you can identify the failure, then a coding agent can often propose a change and test whether it helps.

The harder part is specifying what success means. If you have a reliable evaluation, you can automate quite a bit of that loop. If you’re judging every output by looking at it and saying, ‘That seems better,’ automation becomes much more difficult.

So I expect the engineering effort required to build these systems to come down substantially. But understanding the problem, choosing useful evaluations, and deciding which errors matter will continue to require human judgment.
